scenes.name: James Brown, el Padrino del Soul
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El centro de todo el funk. Tras la muerte de Malcolm X, ningún líder hablaba a las masas negras desposeídas como él: venía de los más pobres, su política no era militante pero su hombría sí; capturó la rabia con su «New Bag», ayudó a contenerla tras el asesinato de King en 1968 y fue la representación completa del hombre negro: político, triunfador, sexual, guerrero, «Black and Proud». Su banda soltó «la Bomba»: R&B rítmico despojado que cargaba el acento en el primer tiempo del compás, «on the One», y rellenaba todo lo demás sin dejar huecos, un agujero negro que atrajo hacia sí la música del mundo y conectó con África. Sus ecos llegaron al reggae, a los congueros del jazz y el soul, a la fusión de Miles Davis, Herbie Hancock o Donald Byrd, a «Superstition», «Inner City Blues» y «Cloud Nine», a las discotecas de Europa y Japón y, a través del sampler, al rap: «The Payback» fue el sample del año en 1992.

podcast.title: Dropping The Platters from Federal
podcast.body: Due to their lack of recording success, Ralph Bass and Federal Records made the decision to drop The Platters from the label, believing they would not achieve anything. "Fed will drop them, as it looked likely they were going to do nothing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Initial Disbelief in The Platters' Talent
podcast.body: Ralph Bass, despite signing The Platters to Federal Records, did not believe they were any good in their early stages, reflecting their initial struggles before their later breakthrough. "nobody Ralph Bass included, thought they were any good."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Producer for Federal Records
podcast.body: Ralph Bass worked for Federal Records as a producer, notably producing singer Linda Hayes, and was responsible for signing The Flamingos (who would become The Platters) to the label. "Ralph Bass, who was currently working for federal records, producing, among other artists, a singer called Linda Hayes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rush Release of Original "Only You"
podcast.body: After The Platters found massive success with Mercury, Ralph Bass and Federal Records controversially rush-released the "awful" original recording of "Only You" in an attempt to cash in, leading to a legal battle with Book Ram and Mercury. "Federal rush released the awful original recording to Cachean and Ram and Mercury took them to court."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Visionary A&R Man
podcast.body: Ralph Bass was a visionary A&R man who signed The Famous Flames to Federal Records. He was exceptionally confident in "Please Please Please," championing the song against strong opposition from his boss, Sid Nathan. Brown's autobiography even suggests Bass was fired and rehired due to the song's success, highlighting his conviction. "Bass was absolutely convinced that please, please, please would be a hit and championed the flames in the face of opposition from his boss, Sid Nathan."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
